content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has released the second edition of its consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis (TB) prevention, focusing on TB preventive treatment (TPT). This updated guidance builds upon and replaces previous recommendations for the programmatic management of TB preventive treatment (PMTPT). It incorporates the latest evidence, particularly regarding TPT for individuals exposed to multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB), and updates recommendations on systematic TB screening and testing for TB infection (TBI). The guidelines emphasize that TB infection (TBI) is a state of persistent immune response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens without clinical evidence of active TB disease. Approximately one-fourth of the global population is estimated to be infected with TB. TPT is a critical intervention recommended by WHO to achieve the End TB Strategy targets, as endorsed by the United Nations High-Level Meeting on TB in September 2023. TPT is part of a broader framework of preventive actions, including TB disease screening, infection control, care for people with HIV and other comorbidities, access to universal healthcare, social protection, and poverty alleviation. The primary audience for these guidelines includes health ministry staff, policymakers working on TB, HIV, infectious diseases, maternal and child health, and technical partners supporting national programs. The second edition aims to provide clarity and incorporate new evidence into its recommendations. Key updates include: 1. Alignment of TPT for MDR/RR-TB: The recommendation for TPT in MDR/RR-TB was updated to align with the population, intervention, comparator, and outcomes (PICO) framework and evidence reviewed by the Guideline Development Group (GDG) in December 2023. 2. Integration of TB symptom screening and TPT: Two recommendations on TB symptom screening in adults and adolescents with HIV were merged to streamline implementation alongside TPT. 3. Introduction of new diagnostic tools: A recommendation was added for the use of new Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigen-based tests for TBI, published by WHO in 2022. 4. Inclusion of new screening tools: Recommendations from the 2021 WHO TB screening guidelines were incorporated, including newly recommended screening tools and TB screening for household contacts and other high-risk groups. 5. Refinement of TPT regimens: A previous recommendation on TPT regimens was divided into two categories: strongly recommended regimens and conditionally recommended alternative options. 6. Withdrawal of outdated recommendations: Two recommendations were withdrawn due to being outdated or difficult to interpret. These included systematic testing and treatment of TBI in people with diabetes, alcohol use, tobacco smoking, and underweight individuals, as well as the provision of 36 months of isoniazid for people with HIV in high TB transmission settings. 7. Terminology updates: The text of nine recommendations was revised to reflect current terminology. 8. Revised management algorithm: The algorithm for managing TPT in contacts, people with HIV, and other risk groups was updated to include new screening and testing options for TBI. 9. Removal of drug dosage details: TPT regimen drug dosages were removed from the guidelines and will now appear in the second edition of the WHO operational handbook on TB preventive treatment. 10. Incorporation of recent evidence: The guidelines were updated with the latest references and evidence, including data on the co-administration of rifapentine with dolutegravir and the safety of rifapentine and levofloxacin. 11. Updated research gaps: Research gaps were revised to reflect the latest evidence reviewed. The guidelines were developed through collaboration among experts in public health policy, TB program management, and clinical care. The recommendations were formulated by successive Guideline Development Groups (GDGs) convened by WHO, with the most recent meeting held in December 2023. The production and writing of the guidelines were coordinated by WHO staff under the direction of the WHO Global Tuberculosis Programme. The guidelines also acknowledge the contributions of external reviewers, evidence reviewers, and funding organizations, including the US Agency for International Development (USAID), the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), and Unitaid. The recommendations aim to provide clear, evidence-based guidance to support national TB programs in reducing the burden of TB and achieving global TB elimination targets.
